newsitem.title: USA: USDA RAISES 97/98 SUGAR FORECAST TO 7.6 MLN TONS.
newsitem.headline: USDA RAISES 97/98 SUGAR FORECAST TO 7.6 MLN TONS.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department on Tuesday raised its forecast of the 1997/98 U.S. sugar crop to 7.67 million short tons, raw value, up slightly from its previous forecast and 5.7 percent above estimated production for the current marketing year.
In its monthly world supply-and-demand report, USDA pegged 1997/98 U.S. sugar beet production at 4.3 million short tons, unchanged from last month and up 6 percent from 1996/97.
The department forecast 1997/98 U.S. sugar cane production at 3.36 million short tons, up 2.7 percent from its July forecast and 5.1 percent higher than 1996/97.
In the coming weeks, USDA must decide how much foreign raw cane sugar to allow to enter the U.S. under an annual quota that begins October 1.
USDA set the quota at 2.31 million short tons in 1996/97, based on a "stocks-to-use" ratio target of 15.5 percent.
That ratio compares stocks on hand at the end of the marketing year to annual consumption.
In comments filed last week with USDA, sugarbeet and sugarcane growers urged the department to use a stocks-to-use ratio of 13.5 percent to determine the annual quota.
That would require USDA to set a smaller import quota than a 15.5 percent ratio target would allow.
At the same time, U.S. sugar users and cane refiners have urged USDA to raise the stocks-to-use target to at least 16.5 percent for 1997/98.
USDA aides have said they could make a decision on the size of the 1997/98 import quota by the end of this month. However, the department's official deadline is September 17.
In Tuesday's report, USDA also raised its estimate of 1997/98 domestic deliveries to 9.90 million short tons, up from the July estimate of 9.75 million.
The higher demand figure, which is 2.1 percent up from the 1996/97 estimate of 9.75 million short tons, offsets some of the increased production forecast by USDA.
